body.p: Applicant submits this Reply in response to the Office Action mailed July 17, 2024 (the "Office Action").
I. Status of the Claims

By this Reply, Applicant amends claims 1, 8, and 15. No claims have been added or cancelled. The originally filed specification and drawings fully support the subject matter of the amended claims. Claims 1-20 are pending in this application. Claims 1, 8, and 15 are the sole independent claims. II. Statement on Substance of Interview

Applicant thanks Primary Examiner Thomas H Hennry for the courtesies extended during the telephonic interview of September 30, 2024. The above amendments and remarks provided below are consistent with the issues discussed during the interview. Agreement was reached that the amendments appear to overcome the rejection, however further search and consideration may be required. III. Section 101 Rejections

Applicant respectfully traverses the rejection of claims 1-20 under 35 U.S.C. § 101 as allegedly being directed to an abstract idea without significantly more, for at least the following reasons. Additionally, as discussed during the Examiner Interview on September 30, 2024, the proposed claim amendments appear to overcome the rejection under 35 U.S.C. § 101.
i) The claimed steps are not "Mental Processes" and are in fact
additional elements that illustrate integration into the practical
application
The Office Action alleges that the claims are directed to the "mental process"
groupings of abstract ideas. (Office Action at p. 3.)
The Office Action also alleges that the claims "additional elements do not
integrate the recited judicial exception into a practical application of the exception."
(Office Action at p. 3.) Applicant respectfully disagrees. However, to expedite
prosecution, Applicant has amended Claim 1. Claim 1 now recites, in part:

recording, by a computing system, tracking data corresponding to one or more motions of a plurality of players or one or more objects via at least one of: one or more cameras or one or more radio frequency identification (RFID) tags for a plurality of holes for a plurality of golf tournaments, wherein the tracking data comprises a distance of each hole of the plurality of holes and a par associated with each hole of the plurality of holes;
utilizing, by the computing system, a clustering algorithm to cluster the plurality of holes into a plurality of hole clusters based on a hole type corresponding to each of the plurality of holes;
analyzing, by the computing system, the tracking data for each of the
plurality of holes and the corresponding hole type to generate a strokes gained metric for each of the hole type;

adjusting, by the computing system, the strokes gained metric for each hole type based on a field of strength metric associated with each of the plurality of golf tournaments, the field of strength metric representing a strength of a player field in a corresponding golf tournament; and
generating, by the computing system, a ranking of the plurality of players based on the adjusted strokes gained metric.
(Emphases added).
For example, "recording, by a computing system, tracking data corresponding to
one or more motions of a plurality of players or one or more objects via at least one of:
one or more cameras or one or more radio frequency identification (RFID) tags for a
plurality of holes for a plurality of golf tournaments, wherein the tracking data comprises
a distance of each hole of the plurality of holes and a par associated with each hole of
the plurality of holes," "utilizing, by the computing system, a clustering algorithm to
cluster the plurality of holes into a plurality of hole clusters based on a hole type
corresponding to each of the plurality of holes," and "analyzing, by the computing
system, the tracking data for each of the plurality of holes and the corresponding hole
type to generate a strokes gained metric for each of the hole type," are not mental
processes. They are therefore additional elements. These additional elements must be
considered for "integration...into a practical application." Applicant respectfully submits
that these are in fact limitations that are clearly integrated into the practical application.
In addition, 2019 Patent Eligibility Guidance emphasizes that "using the
exception in a meaningful way beyond merely linking to the technical environment"
demonstrates integration into the practical application. (PEG at Page 55.) For
example, the steps of independent claim 1 have been amended to recite:

utilizing, by the computing system, a clustering algorithm to cluster the plurality of holes into a plurality of hole clusters based on a hole type corresponding to each of the plurality of holes;

Independent claims 8 and 15 are amended in a substantially similar manner.
These steps are clearly using the alleged exception in a meaningful way beyond merely linking to the technical environment.

The 2019 Patent Eligibility Guidance also emphasizes that "examiners are reminded that a claim that includes conventional elements may still integrate an exception into a practical application, thereby satisfying the subject matter eligibility requirement of Section 101." (Id.) Thus, claim elements may be well-understood, routine, and/or conventional, yet still be integrated into the practical application and thus be patent-eligible.
Accordingly, Applicant requests reconsideration and withdrawal of the Section 101 rejections on at least these grounds.
ii) The Office Action does not contain sufficient reasoning regarding
"well-understood, routine, conventional elements."

On May 4, 2016, the U.S. Patent Office released a memorandum ("the May Memorandum") detailing the requirements of a proper 35 U.S.C. 101 rejection. The May Memorandum requires that "the rejection should explain why the courts have recognized, or those in the field would recognize, the additional elements when taken both individually and as a combination to be well-understood, routine, conventional activities." (Pages 1-2.) Further, the 2019 Revised Patent Subject Matter Eligibility Guidance ("2019 PEG") states that the "analysis of well-understood, routine, conventional activity is done in Step 2B." The 2019 PEG also states that "examiners should continue to consider in Step 2B whether an additional element or combination of elements . . . Adds a specific limitation or combination of limitations that are not well-
understood, routine, conventional activity in the field." The Office Action does not contain sufficient reasoning in this regard.

The U.S. Patent Office released a memorandum on April 19, 2018, entitled "Changes in Examination Procedure Pertaining to Subject Matter Eligibility, Recent Subject Matter Eligibility Decision (Berkheimer v. HP, Inc.)"("Berkheimer Memo"), which analyzes Berkheimer v. HP Inc., 881 F.3d 1360 (Fed. Cir. 2018). The Berkheimer Memo instructs that "[w]hether something is well-understood, routine, and conventional to a skilled artisan at the time of the patent . . .must be based upon a factual determination that is supported .. ." on the record. (Emphasis added.) The Berkheimer Memo clarifies that "an examiner should conclude that an element (or combination of elements) represents well-understood, routine, conventional activity only when the examiner can readily conclude that the element(s) is widely prevalent or in common use in the relevant industry." (Emphasis added.) Such an element need be "so well-known that it need not be described in detail in the patent specification." Conversely, the Office Action is alleging claim features that are described in detail in the patent specification to be "well-understood, routine, and conventional...."

The Berkheimer Memo further cautions that "showing that additional elements are obvious under 35 U.S.C. § 103, or even that they lack novelty under 35 U.S.C. § 102, is not by itself sufficient to establish that the additional elements are well- understood, routine, conventional activities or elements to those in the relevant field." (Emphasis added.)
The Berkheimer Memo requires that rejections alleging that elements are well- understood, routine or conventional must disclose one or more of the following:
1. An admission made by the Applicant that the element(s) are well- understood, routine or conventional.
2. One or more citations of a court decision discussed in the MPEP noting
the well-understood, routine, conventional nature of the element(s).
3. One or more citations to a publication that demonstrates the well- understood, routine, conventional nature of the element(s). The
Berkheimer Memo notes that this publication must not be obscure and that
"merely finding the additional element in a single patent or published
application would not be sufficient . . .unless [it] demonstrates that the
additional element are widely prevalent ...."
The Office Action may contain a statement of official notice, but only in limited
circumstances. If challenged by Applicant, the Office Action must provide evidence per items 1-3.

The Office Action does not comport with these requirements, and does not appear to contain a discussion of these issues. Applicant further asserts that the limitations recited in the claims are not "well-understood, routine or conventional," and accordingly respectfully requests reconsideration and allowance of the claims. Applicant further traverses any official notice that has been used in the rejection, and requests, if the rejections are maintained, detailed factual support.
Accordingly, Applicant respectfully requests reconsideration of the Section 101 rejections, and allowance of the instant application on at least these grounds. IV. Conclusion

The Office Action contains characterization of the claims and the related art with which the Applicant does not necessarily agree. Unless expressly noted otherwise, Applicant declines to subscribe to any statement or characterization in the Office Action.
In discussing the specification, claims, and drawings in this Reply, it is to be
understood that Applicant is in no way intending to limit the scope of the claims to any exemplary embodiments described in the specification or abstract and/or shown in the
drawings. Rather, Applicant is entitled to have the claims interpreted broadly to the maximum extent permitted by statute, regulation, and applicable case law.

In view of the foregoing remarks, Applicant submits that this claimed invention is neither anticipated nor rendered obvious in view of the prior art references cited against this application. Applicant therefore requests the reconsideration and reexamination of the application, and the timely allowance of the pending claims.
